title: Comprehensive functional phenotyping of trigeminal neurons innervating temporomandibular joint (TMJ) tissues in male, female and aged mice, primates, and humans with and without TMJ disorders (TMJD)..
text:
The primary objective of this project is to enhance the processing of human samples and to
implement advanced analytical methodologies, thereby augmenting the scientific impact of the
parent project and RE-JOIN Program. The first aim of the supplement focuses on expanding
sample processing, which necessitates additional consumables and sequencing-related
expenditures. The second aim supports the application of advanced analytical methods, which
require increased personnel effort and computational expertise due to their complexity and time-
intensive nature.

title: Neutralizing antibody pressure on the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 variants."
text:
The SARS-CoV-2 virus continues to evolve, causing repeated waves of infections through the accumulation of
mutations that enable evasion of existing immune responses, yet it remains challenging both to predict which
mutations will arise and to design vaccines that adequately protect against future strains. The proposed project
will use replication-competent pseudoviruses and controlled immunizations of mice to build and test a
lab-based model for predicting SARS-CoV-2 evolution, and to choose promising new vaccine candidates. This
work will enhance our ability to forecast and mitigate the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and other antigenically
variable pathogens.

title: Functional organization and plasticity of the oxytocin system for single or communal parenting in mice
text: (Project 1, Co-PIs: Froemke, Lin, Buzsaki) Oxytocin is a neuropeptide important for social behavior, such as maternal care, pair bonding, and cooperation by partners and groups. Direct axonal oxytocin release into various forebrain targets is critical for social behavior, but it remains unclear if the oxytocin system is heterogeneous and reflects important functional differences for certain cell subsets, relates to inter-animal differences in parental abilities, and if experience-dependent plasticity can adapt the oxytocin system to social and parental environments. Oxytocin administration might also be clinically promising for autism spectrum disorders, social anxiety, and post-partum conditions. However, it is imperative to understand what aspects of oxytocin release relate to parenting, cooperating, and communal living, and whether there are differences in oxytocin modulation that depend on sex, experience, or social context. Here we will address this critical knowledge gap. Recently, with the U19 Behavior Core we built a system for neural recordings and behavioral monitoring, continuously collecting data over days to months on home cage life as mice parent or co-parent together. This was combined with photo-tagged recordings in vivo of identified oxytocin neurons in maternal mice. Our documentary-style video recordings revealed previously-undescribed behavioral interactions by which experienced mothers seemed to encourage or perhaps ‘teach’ co-housed pup- naïve virgin females to engage in maternal care. These behaviors activated photo-tagged oxytocin cells in virgin PVN, providing a robust foundation for the current Project, in which our team aims to understand what aspects of maternal care- by single mothers, pairs, and small groups- activate oxytocin neurons, require oxytocin signaling, and might produce or depend on plasticity of this system upon transition to parenting. The central hypothesis is that the oxytocin system is attuned to social variables related to pup care and the behavior of other potential co-parents, to regulate the behavior of single and co-parents to assure pup survival. We further hypothesize that this depends on adult dominance interactions (studied with Project 2 and analyzed with the Computational Modeling Core) that set up social structures for effective co-parenting. We will monitor oxytocin neurons with in vivo and in vitro electrophysiology, photometry, and perform behavioral and opto-/chemo-genetic studies in adult mice to determine when and how oxytocin modulates neural circuits for social information processing and reliable maternal behavior, with mechanisms of modulation informed by Project 3 and relevant brain areas for social information processing identified in Projects 2 and 4. In Aim 1 we study initial plasticity of oxytocin cells when animals become single mothers, relating oxytocin cell firing to variables such nest building or pup temperature. In Aim 2, we ask if oxytocin neurons help experienced dams teach co-housed naive adults to co-parent. In Aim 3, we study groups of 3-4 mice (including an experienced dam and litter) to quantify dynamics of communal living and co-parenting, and how oxytocin helps ensure social network stability for raising infants.

title: Interplay of inherent promiscuity and specificity in protein biochemical function with applications to drug discovery and exome analysis
text:
Despite notable progress in biology, spurred partly by artificial intelligence (AI), many complex diseases remain
incurable, and the pace of successful drug discovery has stagnated. This project addresses these limitations by
illuminating the interrelationships of diseases, drawing on a deeper understanding of their shared molecular
mechanisms—including the pivotal role of metabolomics— to develop precision medicine AI algorithms that
connect genotype and epigenetics to phenotype, informed by knowledge of the order in which an individual’s
comorbid diseases likely occur. Then, AI algorithms will guide more targeted interventions against key driver
proteins, ultimately enabling more successful, patient specific treatments.

title: Mechanism of Eph-ephrin Signaling in Intestinal Regeneration
text:
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects approximately 3 million Americans and costs the health care system
more than 20 billion dollars annually. Despite recent advances in biological therapy, mortality rate of IBD remains
high at 1.8% annually. The aim of this study is to better understand how cells communicate with each other
during intestinal healing with the hope to use this knowledge to help devise better treatments and improve the
outcomes of IBD patients and reduce the cost of IBD on our healthcare system.

title: Methods for Quantitative Neuroimaging of Tau Burden in Pre-symptomatic AD
text:
The goal of this application is to develop innovative technologies that improve the in vivo quantification of
hyperphosphorylated tau using PET imaging and enhance its utility in both research and eventual clinical
settings. Once validated, we anticipate that our methodology could be readily adapted for application to other
existing or newly reported tau imaging agents.

title: Polyploidy and Sex Dimorphism in a Drosophila Tumor Model
text:
The proposed research employs a straightforward and highly reproducible Drosophila tumor model to
investigate the involvement of polyploidy and sex dimorphism in tumor growth and progression. Successful
execution of this study will enhance our understanding of intratumor ploidy heterogeneity and provide better
strategies for cancer prevention and treatment that consider sex differences.

title: Nevada IDeA Networks of Biomedical Research Excellence
text:
The Nevada IDeA Network for Biomedical Research Excellence (INBRE) program enhances Nevada’s
biomedical research, training, and infrastructure by mentoring early-stage investigators, supporting research
Cores, fostering regional collaborations, and providing student research opportunities. These activities
strengthen the culture of research and the biomedical workforce in Nevada.

title: Allogenic Viral Specific Engineered T Cell for treatment of PML
text:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a devastating brain infection caused by JC virus (JCV) in
immunocompromised individuals for which there are currently no effective antiviral therapies. The aims of this
study are to identify and isolate JCV specific T cell receptors (TCRs) from diverse class I HLA healthy donors
and to validate the ability of T cells expressing these TCRs to clear JCV infection. The ultimate goal is to develop
a therapy that is based on the dominant class I HLA backgrounds in the general population, in order to develop
safer and more effective PML therapy.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of TOX-mediated Programming of CD8 T Cell Exhaustion
text:
Chronic viral infections and cancer are leading causes of morbidity and mortality, but are difficult to treat because
responding virus- or tumor-specific T cells become characteristically dysfunctional, or “exhausted.” Since these
T cell responses are key determinants of clinical outcomes in these diseases, “immunotherapies” targeting these
exhausted T cells have been developed and reduce disease severity for some patients. To improve current
limitations in immunotherapy efficacy and develop new therapy strategies, this proposal seeks to resolve key
mechanistic details of how exhausted T cell function is restrained in these diseases.

title: Reconstruction-free three dimensional positron emission imaging
text:
Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging with radiotracers is used in hospitals around the world
for several applications, including cancer staging and response to treatment assessment, and also is
an important tool in biomedical research for investigating a wide range of health and disorders. The
raw data collected by a PET scanner does not immediately produce an image and is instead
reconstructed from a series of angular views using a tomographic reconstruction algorithm, but
theoretically, the physics does allow for directly producing an image provided the detectors are
sufficiently fast to determine the detection time difference of the photons with resolution of less than 25
picoseconds. In this proposal we aim to develop ultra-fast instrumentation and supporting
computational algorithms leading to the first demonstration of a reconstruction-free imaging system for
cross-sectional imaging of radiotracers.

title: An ensemble framework for regulatory variant prediction.
text:
This research proposal aims to develop an improved computational framework to discover non-
coding functional variants in the human genome and evaluate their contribution to human
diseases in a tissue- and cell-type-resolved manner. We will build machine-learning ensemble
models to predict regulatory variants using existing and emerging epigenomic data and validate
our prediction experimentally. The new method developed in this study will help us to uncover
underlying genetic and molecular mechanisms of human diseases.

title: Activating Low-Affinity T Cells to Prevent Relapse in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
text:
Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is the most common childhood cancer, with relapse remaining a
significant cause of mortality. The BCR-ABL fusion protein drives leukemogenesis in ALL, but current therapies
often fail to sustain effective immune responses due to T cell exhaustion and immunosuppression. The
proposed studies will elucidate whether activating low-affinity T cells specific to the BCR-ABL fusion peptide
can generate durable anti-leukemia immunity, potentially reducing relapse rates.

title: Core C - Biomarker and Biobanking Core
text: Core C: Biomarker and Biobanking Core—Abstract The Biomarker and Biobanking Core will provide scientific direction and oversight of biomarker and biobanking samples for the entire Health, Aging and Dementia in South Africa: A Longitudinal Study (HAALSI) Program. The Core is led by two Co-PIs who will oversee a group of international experts in the fields of epidemiology, genomics, bioinformatics, epigenetics, biostatistics, and biomarker analysis. A biomarker is defined by NIH as a characteristic that is objectively measured and evaluated as an indicator of normal biological processes, pathogenic processes, or pharmacologic responses to a therapeutic intervention. We further divide biomarkers into two broad categories for the purpose of Core C: (1) those that do not require a biological sample to be collected and/or stored (e.g., imaging, blood pressure); and (2) those that require a biological sample to be further analyzed, whether at the point of care (e.g., blood glucose) or in a laboratory (e.g., urine sodium, DNA).This Core will allow us to continue our commitment to longitudinal sample collection in Agincourt and the coordinated use of biomarkers across all four research projects. The proposed HAALSI National survey will augment the HAALSI Agincourt local study with biomarker data from a nationally representative cohort. The growing collection of baseline and new biomarker data related to dementia, cognitive function, cardiometabolic diseases, HIV, and inflammation will inform many research questions and provide opportunities for comparative data for analyses. In particular, we are collecting and analyzing novel biomarkers for dementia and heart failure that have not been measured extensively in African populations. Understanding how to harmonize these biomarkers and trends with the United States Health and Retirement Study biomarker data will be beneficial to understanding the US aging population. Neuroimaging and plasma samples for amyloid beta (Aβ), phosphorylated tau (p-tau), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) will allow for improved phenotyping and relationships between risk factors for dementia. Further, novel cardiac biomarkers of echocardiography and plasma levels of NT-pro brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), cardiac troponin I, and Galactin-3 will be measured for longitudinal evaluation for the first time in an African cohort, allowing for improved phenotyping and risk stratification for cardiometabolic disease morbidity and mortality.

title: Leveraging human genetics to decipher B cell activation dysregulation in lupus
text:
Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease among the most difficult to control. This project aims to uncover
how genetic risk variants for lupus contribute to B cell dysfunction, which drives the disease, by using
advanced genomics and CRISPR-based approaches. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying
B cell activation dysregulation in lupus will guide the development of more effective therapies for lupus
and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

title: AIM-AI: an Actionable, Integrated and Multiscale genetic map of Alzheimer's disease via deep learning
text:
Large amounts of molecular, neuroimaging, biomarker and clinical data have been generated in the context of
Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but the wide range of causal factors for AD have not always been connected to the
methods for tracking the disease etiology or to possible treatments. To process the diverse genetic causes of
AD into useful information for other researchers, in this proposal we assemble an interdisciplinary team to
develop and implement a robust artificial intelligence (AI) framework, namely AIM-AI, for transforming the genetic
catalog of AD in a way that is Actionable, Integrated and Multiscale, so that genetic factors have clear utility for
subsequent studies focusing on cognitive systems. The successful completion of this project will generate a
robust AIM-AI framework, including machine learning methods and tools, resources, and scientific discoveries,
which will be immediately shared with AD researchers and other complex disease research communities.

title: Precision magnetic hyperthermia by integrating magnetic particle imaging
text:
Precision magnetic hyperthermia by integrating magnetic particle imaging
Magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (MIONPs) offer considerable potential for numerous biomedical applications.
Our objective is to develop an integrated magnetic particle imaging/magnetic fluid hyperthermia workflow that
incorporates imaging-guided treatment planning for small animal models.

title: Optimizing Clinical Documentation Quality to Reduce Health Disparities in Home Healthcare: The ENGAGE Study
text: Documentation quality in clinical settings varies significantly across patient populations, contributing to health disparities and affecting care delivery for racial and ethnic minority patients. This project aims to design and pilot-test a technology-driven system, ENGAGE, that will help to optimize documentation quality and identify patterns that impact care quality among home healthcare nurses. Achieving this goal will improve the quality of care and reduce health disparities for patients treated in home healthcare settings.

title: Liposome-displayed ApoB fragment for active immunotherapy against atherosclerosis
text:
Although lipid-lowering therapeutics like statins offer benefit, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)
remains the leading cause of mortality in the US. ASCVD is primarily a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory
disease, therefore immune modulating treatments hold potential to rationally address the underlying cause. This
proposal focuses on developing a peptide vaccine that elicits strong CD8+ T cell response, which ideally will
result in reductions in atherosclerotic lesion size or stabilization of atherosclerotic plaques.

title: Understanding the contribution of BCL11A to neuron function and neurological disease
text:
Patients with BCL11A mutations exhibit a range of clinically challenging phenotypes including intellectual
disability, social deficits, and epilepsy. Our preliminary data suggest that BCL11A plays an important role in the
function of GABAergic interneurons, which are responsible for the regulation of neuronal inhibition in the brain.
We will use multiple experimental approaches to establish the contribution of BCL11A to human neuron
development and function, and mouse models will be used to establish the mechanisms by which BCL11A
dysfunction leads to the observed clinical abnormalities.
